author: @elkingthemc
text: This seems like more of a style clash that boils down to personal preference. If you're into clever and witty punchlines, you'll probably lean towards Drake. If you're more into deep psychoanalysis and storytelling, Kendrick's your guy. And if you already dislike Drake, his fans, or the idea that he represents what's wrong with hip-hop, then Kendrick can do no wrong in your eyes anyway. I think George’s critique of Kendrick’s breakdown was that, while the psychoanalysis was complex, the delivery was pretty straightforward and didn’t offer much lyrical complexity beyond that. Overall, this beef gave us some amazing art from both sides, and it’s a shame that the culture was too narrow-minded to appreciate the back-and-forth without taking sides. People were actually unsubscribing just because George and Ryan had a different opinion. So much for being free thinkers, right? It’s wild that some are assuming things about Ryan just because he didn’t vibe with Kendrick’s approach and delivery. Smh. Keep it up, guys. Great breakdown as always! At the end of the day, it’s just a matter of style preference—or whether you're just not a Drake fan 😂.

author: @DerekFernandes-l9j
text:
Just stumbled on this 10 months later.  Guys are just giving their opinions, which is respectable and what this channel is about.  It's extremely hard to be un-biased in music.  So, comments, don't have to rag on them if their opinions don't match yours.  However, LIV, couple objective points regarding why the comments are what they are:

1. Sonically. Drake might be the best ever regarding how his voice sounds on tracks.  Which is partly what makes him so good.  And although mentioned in earlier reaction about how we grade diss tracks, be it bars, sound, etc, the impression you are giving is that the sonic part is much more important than the bars.  As an example that comes to top-of-mind, this was extremely evident with your reaction to Drake's line in Pushups: "it's the bark with the bite".  Based on your grading scale of double-entrendas and witty lines, this objectively falls short.   However the facial reactions says otherwise.  I'd suggest that being up-front about scaling your grading scale versus asking your subscribers how to grade it, and then reacting to it the way you did, would have helped a ton. 

1B (sub note):  Even though the song is objectively fantastic, I couldn't bring myself to watch your Family Matters reaction video because the bias was difficult to internalize.  I'm curious if your reactions to Drake's allegations to Kendrick were similar to Kendrick's allegations against Drake, as in this reaction video?  I'm not here to debate the merits of either allegations or to spark a debate over them, but to be unbiased, by definition, means to react similar in similar situations.  Which further proves the point of sonic preference.  Again, I didn't watch the Family Matters reaction, and I don't want to assume, but I feel like the reactions were more receptive in that video.  

2. Change.  Cars change, clothes change, sports and their rules change, the internet changes, etc.  So too, it shouldn't be out of question to establish that battle rap changes - could argue whether it "should" change however.  The impression you gave was grading this based on the traditional "diss" which provided a bias view-point in your reactions.  Drake's songs better aligned with that narrative.  However, does that make it more effective?  Let's take a look at football for example.  Today, if a team was running Iso 25 times/game, as was common in the 80's/90's, it more than likely would not be effective based on how teams manage modern-day defenses.  However, if a football historian were to watch that, they might resonate and appreciate that more than a modern-day offense.  Generally, people know what they know and it's always extremely difficult to see other perspectives and conceptualize/agree with them.  

3. Time. To me, this was the first of its kind - being that its online presence was insane.  Mainly due to the surge in reactors and live-streamers, it was easy to "live-in-the-monent" versus listening to it the next day, or days after.  The angle here was very strategic, and based on the arguments above, that "should" now be a topic of debate regarding how to evaluate a diss - maybe?  The intent was to take the sails out of Family Matters, which I would argue that it did.  The song doesn't have the same effect if not listened to in-the-moment.  People who heard it live, it's effective because it's already ingrained in them; they lived it.  Listening to it after, it doesn't have the same effect.  An example might be basketball where the game looks much more difficult in-person versus on television.  So going to a game and watching something spectacular, that person has a different perspective than someone who just watched the highlight on television say a week after.  They lived it.  

4. Grading scale.  It seemed as if the same level of scrutiny against Kendrick's bars weren't there for Drake.  Presumably because everyone went into this battle with the assumption that Kendrick's word-play would be phenomenal?  And honestly that's life - as an example, you can't expect a new-grad employee to provide the same effort and care into a business as the CEO.  You'd naturally expect the CEO to work longer hours, make tougher and quicker decisions,  be more ingrained in the business, etc.  However, to be un-biased means the exact opposite.  I would argue it's impossible to not be biased in a battle rap, honestly.  Everyone always predicts a winner beforehand. So doing these videos I can't even imagine how difficult it was to try and remain un-biased.  So I'd argue that if you pre-empted by saying "I think Drake will win this battle because of "x,y,z", that would have helped the audience reactions.  I understand the channel is about being objective, but a battle rap isn't.  It comes with a lot of emotion, as does music in general.  But a battle rap even more-so.  If we saw a 1-1 with Jordan/Lebron, both in their primes, I very highly doubt people would be objective about it.  

I agree that music-wise, bar-wise, along with your other criteria you evaluate disses with, this probably massively fell short.  However, strategically and message-wise, this probably clears Family Matters.  To me, searching for "truths" in rap battles is a bit corny.  But that is part of how this battle unfolded online, like it or not.  Strengthening the above statement about change.  By that grading criteria, Kendrick's allegations are much more believable due to Drake's history.  Albeit he denied one allegation here, Drake's allegations against Kendrick were disproven years ago so not as believable to the general public.  

All that to say, I think people don't understand exactly how hard it is to do what you do, especially related to the un-bias part.  However, what would have helped the reactions you received in the comments would be: A. being more open about grading scales, B. taking criticism better - especially evident in the beginning of the 6:16 reaction with the trolling and condescending attitude (was difficult to watch), and C. tones.  What I mean with tones is that 50% of all language is non-verbal, such as body language.  It was clear that even before each track started, you were more keen to hear Drake than Kendrick.  

I know you probably don't care about a random guy's perspective online, and might probably never even see this, but had to get off my chest.  Hope you guys continue to grow the channel and see more success.  This is simply my retrospective perspectives.
